strengths: Well-motivated benchmark addressing a real gap in agent code security evaluation for repository-level, multi-file tasks with realistic complexity (150K LoC context, 172 edited lines, 77 CWEs across 10 domains)
Thoughtful automated curation pipeline with adaptive masking, description generation, and verification ensuring task integrity and scalability to new vulnerabilities
Significant and striking findings: 80%+ of functionally correct agent solutions are insecure, revealing a critical gap that has practical importance for vibe coding adoption
Comprehensive evaluation across 9 agent/LLM combinations with rigorous metrics (SECPASS ⊥ FUNCPASS) that disentangle security from functional capability
Clear, well-structured presentation with effective figures and concrete qualitative case studies (D.1-D.3) illustrating real security vulnerabilities
Honest discussion of limitations (Python-only, test-based evaluation) and preliminary nature of mitigation strategies
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: curation pipeline applies existing LLM techniques (masking, generation, verification) in a straightforward manner; core insight of using vulnerability fixes as task sources is sensible but not surprising

Security evaluation relies entirely on test-based proxies: average 3.7 tests per task is modest, and test-based evaluation may miss subtle exploits, edge cases, and sophisticated attacks not explicitly tested

Critical absence of human baseline: abstract mentions humans generated vulnerable code on these tasks but provides no quantitative comparison, making it unclear if agent performance is worse than human programmers

Shallow exploration of mitigation strategies (Section 5): only three simple prompting approaches tested with no investigation of root causes, no analysis of why security guidance reduces functionality, and no exploration of alternative approaches (tools, fine-tuning, multi-agent)

Python-only scope limits generalizability across programming languages and security domains with different characteristics (e.g., C/Rust memory safety vulnerabilities differ from Python security concerns)

Curation process dependencies: three curation steps use SWE-Agent itself, creating circular dependency; no ablation study or sensitivity analysis on masking/description quality effects on downstream evaluation

Missing statistical analysis: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests despite evaluating stochastic LLMs; unclear if observed differences between agents are statistically meaningful

Unexplained findings: Gemini 3 Pro shows 195% functional improvement but only 57% security improvement (Table 5), suggesting possible artifacts or "secure by accident" patterns that deserve deeper analysis

strengths: Addresses timely and critical security gap in widespread vibe-coding adoption with concrete evidence that 80%+ of functionally correct agent-generated code contains exploitable vulnerabilities

Well-engineered SUSVIBES benchmark substantially exceeds prior security benchmarks in scope (77 CWEs vs. 13-45), context scale (162K lines), and complexity (multi-file edits, repository-level reasoning)

Comprehensive experimental evaluation spanning 3 agent frameworks × 3 frontier LLMs with stratified CWE analysis revealing complementary model strengths/blindspots and functionality-security decoupling (e.g., Gemini 3 improves functionality 195% but security only 57%)

Rigorous three-stage benchmark construction pipeline with adaptive verification ensuring task descriptions match canonical implementations line-by-line, preventing information leakage from security fixes

Honest analysis of mitigation strategies demonstrating preliminary approaches fail and quantifying the security-functionality trade-off (Figure 8 transition matrix), revealing agents prioritize one objective at expense of other
Concrete vulnerability case studies (Appendix D) with detailed analysis of timing side-channels, CRLF injection, XSS, and session expiration that clearly illustrate security risks agents introduce
weaknesses: Severely limited to Python only—fundamentally undermines generalizability claims about 'vibe coding' as a programming paradigm; security vulnerabilities are language-dependent, and single-language study cannot establish general principles about agent behavior across the ecosystem

Circular methodology: Uses SWE-Agent + Claude to generate masks, descriptions, and verify task quality (Prompts I-III), introducing potential bias and confounding LLM contributions; no ablation or sensitivity analysis on whether different verification models would produce different benchmarks

Security evaluation relies entirely on test adequacy as proxy—critical limitation not adequately addressed: human-written unit tests may systematically miss vulnerability classes (timing side-channels, race conditions, probabilistic failures) and don't guarantee production safety

Shallow root-cause analysis: Paper demonstrates what agents get wrong but not why; doesn't explain why agents miss security despite context, or investigate the fundamental functionality-security decoupling (Gemini 3 results) that warrants deeper investigation

Questionable benchmark representativeness: Real-world vulnerabilities in ReposVul/MoreFixes are human-discovered and human-fixed (selection bias); agents may introduce different vulnerability patterns with different severity distributions, potentially inflating or deflating the measured gap

SECPASS metric conflates functionality and security (secure AND correct / all tasks); the functionality-security trade-off in Section 5 is inadequately analyzed—unclear whether trade-off is fundamental to agent architecture or addressable through training/prompting strategy

Preliminary mitigation strategies are limited and largely negative results: Only three simple strategies tested (generic reminder, self-selection, oracle CWE); no exploration of multi-turn refinement, specialized security models, compositional verification, or why agents fail to identify security risks even with oracle information

Task construction filters toward testable vulnerabilities (requiring test modifications), potentially underrepresenting hard-to-test vulnerabilities (concurrency, timing, scale-dependent, latent) and biasing benchmark toward easier security cases

Experimental design lacks rigor: No significance testing or confidence intervals despite modest sample size (200 tasks); single runs (pass@1); no ablation on default generic security reminder; max steps = 200 (could agents improve with more reasoning?) not investigated; default system prompts not shown

Reproducibility gaps: No explicit commitment to release SUSVIBES; exact evaluation prompts not provided (only system prompts); no analysis of sensitivity to prompt phrasing; Docker preservation unclear; findings depend critically on test suite quality which may vary

strengths: Addresses urgent, timely problem: security of AI-generated code in rapidly-adopted vibe coding paradigm
Rigorous benchmark construction: real-world grounding from actual vulnerability fix commits, 186 tasks spanning 79 CWE types across 10 application domains
Comprehensive empirical evaluation: 12 agentic configurations (3 frameworks × 4 LLMs) with stratified analysis by CWE category and domain; detailed case studies with concrete security implications
Execution-based validation via Docker containerization ensures reproducible functional and security assessment, avoiding false confidence from code inspection alone
Well-designed curation pipeline with multi-stage verification: adaptive task verification, test quality review (6.5% implementation-coupled tests identified and fixed), human expert validation

weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: curation pipeline straightforwardly applies existing techniques (SWE-AGENT for most steps); evaluation uses only standard unit testing without novel security assessment techniques

Test-based evaluation has fundamental unexamined limitations: only 3.5 security tests/task on average; 44% of tests acknowledged to 'may miss edge-case implementations'; no investigation of false negatives or unexplored exploit modalities (e.g., race conditions); security claims depend on test quality not stress-tested

Weak mitigation strategies and shallow root cause analysis: only two trivial strategies tested (self-selection, oracle); oracle CWE hints barely improve security (15.1% vs 11.8%); no systematic investigation of *why* mitigation fails; Table 6 shows agents identify CWE poorly (F1=0.195) but this isn't explored; Figure 4 shows variance across CWE categories without mechanistic explanation

Benchmark scale concerns: only 186 tasks (0.9% yield from 20,000 commits); Python-only; 100 repositories; sparse coverage per CWE category; Table 9 shows dramatic complexity effects (66.9%→30.3% FuncPass for multi-file), suggesting possible hard-case cherry-picking

Insufficient exploration of security-functionality trade-offs: binary pass/fail treats minor timing leaks identically to data exposure; no severity gradation; missing guidance on practical deployment thresholds or when manual review is necessary

Missing baselines and comparisons: no comparison with human programmers, static analysis tools, or prior security-focused code generation work; single pass@1 metric with no significance testing; differences between models (e.g., 12.9% vs 11.8%) not statistically validated

Incomplete root cause analysis: case studies provide examples but not systematic failure mode categorization; no analysis of whether failures stem from instruction following, semantic gaps, training data, or context limitations; inadequate exploration of why prompt-based mitigation fails fundamentally

Experimental design gaps: max steps=200 not justified; no analysis of step efficiency; default system prompts; weak generic security reminder; environment construction uses SWE-AGENT (one of the evaluated agents), introducing potential circularity bias

Reproducibility concerns: code and dataset not provided for review; results depend on specific model versions that may evolve; some prompt templates incomplete; reliance on SWE-AGENT whose behavior may change

Narrow scope limits generalizability: Python-only; 100 repositories; no cross-language or cross-domain transfer analysis; missing ablation studies on pipeline components and impact of task description quality
